title: Community Building
author: Mutually Assured Instruction
summary: The author uses his experience volunteering as a rabbit pace-setter for a local youth cross-country running club to explore what community does for motivation, identity, and sustained effort — then transfers those insights to school classrooms and teacher professional communities. He argues that community makes it easier to do hard things: when your actions impact people you care about and who care about you, you find capacity you didn't know you had. The article identifies a crucial distinction between attachment and genuine community in schools: the classroom where students cry when the teacher leaves reflects dependence, not the kind of community that produces independent learners. He explores the Science of Learning online community as a model of professional community for evidence-based teachers who may be isolated in their own schools. The piece concludes that belonging to a community of people with shared conviction changes not just motivation but what is possible.
points: Community makes it easier to do hard things — when your actions can impact others you care about, you find capacity you did not know you had.
We often mistake attachment for genuine community in schools — the classroom students are reluctant to leave may reflect emotional dependence rather than the kind of belonging that produces learning.
Using inclusive language — 'we are doing so well at elaborating on our points today' — changes the felt sense of community in a classroom in ways that have real consequences for learner motivation.

Prior to engaging with the evidence-based teaching community online, teaching could feel pretty isolating — especially if you were pushing for research-informed practice in a school where that wasn't the norm.
Change in teaching doesn't happen overnight — it happens in small incremental tweaks and iterations over time, and community is what makes those iterations sustainable.
quotes: These same educators would’ve started their career no doubt sinking hours into trying to commit to what they thought at the time was best practice but when what the universities told them was best practice did not actually work and the schools themselves were changing priorities constantly, these teachers ended up putting together a patchwork of strategies that work for them and allow them to get by.

I then went and made this far worse for myself by getting the opportunity to work for a year at one of the best performing schools in the state before returning back to the public sector with a wealth of additional knowledge and passion for education that I was expecting others to both want and appreciate.

This is not necessarily malicious in nature, however the nature of the job and the way in which the goals posts on what schools should be and should do have constantly changed over the past few decades has led to many educators operating in a default state as a protective mechanism.

Carl Hendrick says “you can’t connect the dots if you don’t have any” and connecting with all of these dots has provided a sense of validation and purpose in teaching that may make remaining in a profession which has an enormous rate of attrition more sustainable.

Teaching attracts such a disparate array of personalities and for the first 8 years of my career I always had a very small group of teacher friends, but this was almost always based on shared outside interests and not education itself.

What shocked me even more was that these experts who previously seemed completely outside of the world I existed in, were the most approachable and accessible people possible wanted to engage in and share their knowledge with others.

We will often laud the teachers who’s classes are crying to leave them on the final day and visiting them 24 hours later and showering them with gifts before the teacher who makes their class a team working together towards mastery.
